subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT PROVINCES INQUIRE INTO STATUS OF LANGUAGES UNDER THEIR JURISDICTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion of urgent and pressing necessity.
Given the strong interest that every Canadian has in political development in Quebec and the fact that the white paper published recently by the Quebec government is an important step forward and that this French language charter in Quebec might create a new concept of bilingualism in Canada, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau):
That the federal government urge all the other Canadian provinces to develop as well a white paper on the minority language status within their boundaries as well as on the jeopardy in which the majority language, that is English, finds itself, so that we might properly assess the real status of the French and English languages in Canada.

subsubtopic: DRILLING IN BEAUFORT SEA-RESULT OF DELAY IN PUBLISHING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and it concerns the progress of the Beaufort Sea drilling project. Progress is now going ahead despite the fact that the government has not yet decided whether or not drilling is to go ahead this summer. In view of the fact that the minister assured the House last month, in response to a question of mine on March 23, that he will be able to make a decision by the end of March, will he tell the House whether it is his intention that procrastination on this matter will do for the Beaufort Sea exploration what procrastination on oil and gas regulations has done for northern exploration as a whole?

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEW JOB-CREATING MEASURES FOR QUEBEC AND FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of Finance arises from the Conference Board of Canada forecast published today which indicates that even after an analysis of the implications of the minister's budget, unemployment in Canada will average 7.9 per cent in 1977 and in the province of Quebec will reach the

April 6, 1977
astronomical level of 10 per cent in 1977 meaning some
400,000	Quebecers will be out of work during the coming 12 months. Considering that more than 50 per cent of the new unemployment in Canada in the last two years has already occurred in the province of Quebec and given the implications for national unity of maintaining high levels of employment, has the government at long last reconsidered its position and is it prepared to announce its intention to bring in some new job creation measures, particularly for that province?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEW JOB-CREATING MEASURES FOR QUEBEC AND FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have not constructed the economic policy to deal specifically with one province. We recognize Canada is a single country but that there are regional problems and in the budget we recognized this with more favourable terms for investment tax credits in the Atlantic provinces and parts of Quebec. Indeed, the impact of the direct job creation measures is to favour those particular areas but I do not propose to bring forward specific measures with regard to the province of Quebec alone.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEW JOB-CREATING MEASURES FOR QUEBEC AND FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Considering the disproportionate amount of new unemployment that has occurred in the province of Quebec in the last two years I would have thought it would justify specific measures by the government to deal with it.
Considering that within the next two months there will come on the labour market some 100,000 university students, 60,000 students from community colleges, plus 288,000 who will have left high school, all together about 400,000 young people, I ask the minister if the government has any additional plans to cope with the serious unemployment problem those young people will face this coming summer, since this will be the worst summer for employment for young people in Canada since the great depression.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEW JOB-CREATING MEASURES FOR QUEBEC AND FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is fair to remind the hon. gentleman that we have added another S100 million in direct job creation, to make the total $458 million during the current fiscal year. I also point out to him, and I hope he will think seriously about this, that the best long-run prospect for these young Canadian graduates coming on to the market lies in making a strong addition to Canadian industrial and commercial capacity, thereby creating additional jobs in the private sector.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF NEW JOB-CREATING MEASURES FOR QUEBEC AND FOR YOUNG PEOPLE
speechtext:
A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. If rhetoric could create jobs we would have had full employment months ago. Since the government is doing less now on a comparable basis, given present levels of unemployment, to create jobs than it did in 1971, and since we will have all those young people coming on the job market in a couple of months, is the Minister of Finance really saying today what the Prime Minister said in the University of Toronto two weeks ago, that if young people want jobs they have to leave the country?
Oral Questions

speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. 1 am saying to the hon. gentleman that if young people want jobs, and we want them to be able to secure those jobs, efforts such as his to discourage investment in Canada are working very much against them.

subsubtopic: FINDING OF RADON GAS IN DRINKING WATER ON RED EARTH RESERVE-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Three or four days ago the monthly publication of the Saskatchewan Indians revealed that radioactive radon gas had been found in the drinking water in one of the wells on the Red Earth Indian reserve in Saskatchewan in a concentration some 70 to 225 times higher than the level normally

considered safe. How long has the government known about this situation and what is being done to protect the people living on this reserve? Do they have access to alternative water supplies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FINDING OF RADON GAS IN DRINKING WATER ON RED EARTH RESERVE-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: For some time now, the Indians on the Red Earth reserve have been exploring for radioactive minerals and rare gases on the reserve, particularly uranium and helium. In the course of this exploration they drilled some deep holes and carried out other work. Recently it was found that radon gas had been released and concern was felt about one of the wells, a well near a lumber mill. This was tested by the Department of National Health and Welfare. speechtext:
1. (a) Seven, including four from Cuba, one from the PRC and two from the USSR, (b) During their term of appointment all diplomats are considered persona grata in the eyes of the receiving country. Following "agrement" in the case of the head of mission, or notification in the case of other members of the mission, any action by the receiving state to terminate the appointment indicates that the person concerned is no longer grata in the receiving state. The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations does not leave any other choice. While Article 9 of the Convention refers to the two categories of persona non grata and not acceptable, the latter expression is normally intended to cover non-diplomatic staff, with respect to whom the term persona non grata is not usually employed. Therefore, any diplomat whose recall or expulsion is requested by the receiving country can be considered persona non grata.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Is the government giving any consideration to establishing a consulate or other diplomatic office in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in view of the recent initiative in this respect by the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The topic of a Canadian Consulate in Kiev has been a subject of discussion within the government for many years. At the time the Soviet Union opened their Consulate General in Montreal, it was agreed that the Canadian Government would be free to open one either in Kiev or in Leningrad. While there is much to be said in favour of opening an office in Kiev, we have not, to this time, done so. We must look at issues such as this in terms of global priorities within the framework of the constraints imposed upon us by the government's austerity program. Representatives of the Canadian Embassy in Moscow make periodic trips to the Ukraine and, for the present, seem able to cope with the problems that arise there. We will continue to give consideration to the possibility of opening in Kiev, but we would be less than frank if we did not say that it is unlikely in the near future.

That, when the House adjourns on April 6, 1977, it shall stand adjourned until April 18, 1977, provided that at any time prior to that date if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the government, that the public interest requires that the House should meet at an earlier time during the adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give notice that he is so satisfied, and thereupon the House shall meet at the time stated in such notice, and shall transact its business as if it had been duly adjourned to that time; and
That, in the event of Mr. Speaker's being unable to act owing to illness or other cause, the Deputy Speaker or the Deputy Chairman of Committees shall act in his stead for the purpose of reconvening the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. Before giving the floor to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), I hope I am not being at all presumptuous in saying that should events transpire later this day to give effect to the motion under debate, it will of course be my pleasure, in the usual manner, to receive in the usual room the usual guests for the usual festivities.

Mr. Speaker, I hope you were not intending to change the direction of the remarks 1 was about to make! I must say it is a very tempting situation.
As I was concluding on Friday last, we had talked about the need for more time to be spent in this House rather than seeking an adjournment. Since the weekend there has been Monday and Tuesday to canvass the possibility of any change of heart on the part of the government to produce legislation or to amend what is clearly one of the most inadequate budgets the country has ever seen. I must say I am rather pessimistic at this point that there is going to be any change.
This would have been a useful time for the opposition parties to unite. It is too bad so much time was spent on Friday with one opposition party attacking the official opposition and vice-versa. Quite frankly 1 do not think that adds very much to
(Mr. Smith (Saint-Jean).]
the debate concerning the budget, because it is a government budget. I am quite satisfied that neither the New Democratic Party nor the Conservative party would have brought in this kind of budget. 1 do not think it is a Tory budget. I think it has probably out-toried the Tories. God knows it is not an NDP budget. It seemed to me rather futile to spend a good part of last Friday attacking one another when we should have been in opposition to and fighting the kind of budget we saw come from the other side of the House. I therefore urge my friends to my right to unite with us in opposing a budget which does not respond in any way to the needs of the country in this very desperate time of economic stress.
There is one thing we can be sure of-that we are not facing an election on this budget. What the government has done this year, I predict it will reverse 100 per cent next year. We foresee a budget with personal tax cuts, capital works programs, and a reduction in corporate rip-offs. This will of course give them something popular to run on in the next election.
Hear, hear!
I am glad to see my good friend, Mr. Anderson, cheering that. I can see he is familiar-
Order, please. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) will please refer to hon. members of the House by riding, not by name.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It gave me a chance to remember that the hon. member's riding is Comox-Alberni, one of the finer areas of Vancouver Island. I see he is delighted not to have to run on this budget and that is why he is so spirited this afternoon. I hope the voters in his riding will remember that the budget he supports does nothing for the one million unemployed. That is what the next election will be about, and the kind of phony budget we can expect a year from now will purport to do the things the government should be doing at the moment if it were not so cynical.
During the debate on Friday the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) put a very significant question to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). "What about a deficit? After all, we have limits to what we can do" he said. I think we in this party will agree that we have to be concerned about deficits. You grant $1.2 billion in tax concessions. Instead of forgoing all that money, if you put it into the treasury and reverse it at the other end, and provide it as tax cuts, you would not have to worry about a deficit. You would have reduced the deficit and still would have done a good deal about consumer demand and putting people back to work.
I know I must relate my remarks to the motion before us. The question is, should this House rise this afternoon, or should it not? I am still of the view that it should not rise, although no doubt it will. We should sit here and contemplate.

Meditate on the unemployed.
April 6, 1977

We should meditate for one week at least about those people whose search for work has been futile. I agree with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. McRae) that debate on this question has grown simplistic. It is simplistic for the reason that the government has failed to understand that our unemployment rate is a symptom of the system under which we live. It is a chronic symptom. Mr. Speaker, we have never sought different or new solutions to the problem. Instead we have decided to live with the problem. Continuing concessions to the corporate sector have only resulted over the years in ever higher rates of unemployment. What does the $485 million corporate tax concession mean? Is it a tax incentive for investment? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) quite rightly says, "Oh, but the corporations will not get it unless they invest. They must first put the money out." But the minister did not say that they should spend the money in order to reduce employment, not increase it. If they spend money on capital equipment, on capital intensive investment, they will be able to employ fewer people and enjoy a tax benefit for doing so.
This budget will reward corporations for throwing workers off the assembly line and curtailing their jobs. It is a budget in reverse, a budget which not only will not create more employment but may be instrumental in creating more unemployment, while large corporations are given tax concessions if they spend money. The least the minister could have done was tie those tax concessions to the number of jobs created. His failure to do so is a clear example of the government's negligence, a clear example that the government still fails to understand that there is another approach to the economy besides the chamber of commerce approach. The government must listen to the views of all parts of society. If it listens to the views of only one segment, it will dig this country's grave in terms of unemployment.
As technology grows, so does unemployment, something we have not considered. We ought to consider the question. As society invests more and more money in expensive machinery, in capital intensive projects, so more and more become unemployed. The answer is to use the public sector in order to bring unemployment rates down. 1 say the failure to heed such advice is a symptom of ideological fanaticism, Adam Smith fanaticism, right-wing fanaticism.
Fascism.

The government refuses to accept the other side of the equation, as most countries of western Europe have done for the last 20 years. Those countries have consistently out-performed this country in terms of providing employment for their people. I am thinking of West Germany, Sweden, and all the other countries in that part of the world.
There is lots of unemployment there.

Come off it.
Easter Recess
Order, please. The hon. member for New Westminster has the floor.

The reality of 1977 is that more capital intensive investment results in higher unemployment rates, and by so investing we throw more people on to the garbage heap in Canada, into prisons, into insane asylums, on to skid row. We are saying to them, "We don't need you any more. Because you are not qualified to do one of the new technical jobs, we don't want you. We have no work for you to do." Mr. Speaker, we are automating ourselves out of work, and the government refuses to respond to that reality.
The government's response is: we must increase our competitive position in the world by providing tax incentives to private industry. Mr. Speaker, we have done that for a long time. Eric Kierans not long ago pointed out that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his musings talks about a new society, the business community reacts with a sort of incredible paranoia. The Prime Minister was trying to tell some of our people that we live in a new society,-I have not called it socialism, for the Prime Minister would not use such a term-and the business community's reaction was incredible. But you see, Mr. Speaker, we do live in a new society, no matter how we look at it. Now it is a different society, because the age of the new technology dawned after the Second World War, and our technological achievements have been growing and growing.
Until you accept this new age as a reality, you will not improve this country's unemployment statistics. Oh yes, they will go down to 7 per cent, perhaps up to 8 per cent, and fluctuate somewhat; but too many people will be out of work. We are still telling our young people, unless we take into account the reality of the new society, that we do not need them, we do not want them. We are saying, "Us old guys are still going to run this place, and you young people had best take your place in the lineup for your welfare cheques or your unemployment insurance cheques." That attitude spawns all this country's crime problems, all this country's social disruption.
If you want to hold the country together, put people to work. I say that people have the responsibility to accept work, but first it is the duty of the government to provide jobs our people can accept. The government cannot quite accept that. It does not quite see the picture. In our new society, instead of handing a guy an unemployment cheque, hand him a job. It is the only answer. That is the only way to overcome what is, clearly, a breakdown in the country's social structure.
In the last 100 years we have looked after companies like the CPR. From 1881 to 1970, the company accumulated about $2.3 billion worth of assets. Under the present government, which is allegedly hostile to the business community, the CPR tripled its assets in five years. It took the company one hundred years to accumulate $2.3 billion, but between 1970 and 1975 it increased its assets to $6.2 billion. The same is true of the Royal Bank, Imperial Oil, and other major companies in the private sector. I do not say that is wrong. They are doing their job. It is their job to increase profits for their investors. I
80012-191/2

April 6, 1977
Easter Recess
accept that and respect it. Yet surely to God it is our job to look after all the people, and not just the investors in major corporations. This budget merely looks after that narrow section of the community.
We hear the government talking about tax dividend credits. My God, what about the guy who pays no income tax, has no investments, and cannot buy the products those large corporations are allegedly gearing up to produce? They will not gear up to produce those goods unless there is demand for them. Apparently the government is applying the trickle-down theory. It is providing wealth for people at the top, but doing nothing for the people at the bottom of the scale. They are getting nothing but the crumbs and have no capacity with which to buy goods. If they were able to buy, our economy could get going once more.
In this country we see new patterns of consumption. We must examine the new technology and consider how to apply it to the country's economy. The unkindest cut of all came from hon. members opposite who said that the NDP has no new ideas. My God, you have not even started to use our ideas. Why not try a couple of them? If you do you may find that you will save this free enterprise system you are allegedly trying to protect. Mr. Speaker, we are the best friends the small businessman ever had. We are saying, "Put purchasing power into the hands of those who spend and want to buy something." And what are you guys opposite doing? You are saying, "Oh no, we don't want to help those little guys. We are going to help the fellow who wants to make a couple of million dollars and invest his money."
Mr. Speaker, you have to help the clothier, the butcher, the baker, the candlestick maker, the real estate salesman, and all the other little guys in the economy. This budget does not help them.
Don't forget the farmer.

You have not done this, and that is why the government will not call an election on the strength of this budget.
But the government has done one thing. It has brought those at the summit of the economy back into the Liberal fold. It brought back the large corporations; but then, they have always been in the government's fold.
And Jack Horner.
And Jack, yes.
The budget did it for Jack.
Jack who?

Mr. Speaker, we could do much to improve the economy. We could bring in a capital works program, and ban overtime to spread the work around. A national succession duty law could be brought in so that we would not have gains between the provinces on succession duty and there would be some revenue from unearned income. We could have done

something about the ripoff on capital gains and taxed them as Carter said we should at 100 per cent, just like we do with income.
We could easily have done those kinds of things in the next week but, as I say, I am sure we are going to adjourn this afternoon. That will make everybody happy. We would not be adjourning if the opposition had united. However, we spent so much time attacking each other we forgot where the villains were.
Where are they?
They are on that side. I close by saying this is a sad day for this country when we find the government willing to use a million plus unemployed for the purpose of its re-election in 1978.
Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate that I take up the optimism shown by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) when talking about this adjournment motion. I am not an obstructionist.
Oh, oh!
I am not obstructionist by nature, but things around this place get me very riled up. Parliament is a very unreal place.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The door swings both ways.

That is correct, Mr. Speaker. I do not know what the member opposite has to do. I think he is just here to write birthday cards and get well cards without worrying about the business of this nation. We are here as serious politicians to look at the problems facing the country and to try to solve them through legislation. By and large, all members of the House share that philosophy.
I became very upset recently when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) stood in this House and said we could not afford to attempt to solve the unemployment problem. It should be the other way around. We cannot afford not to solve the unemployment problem. That minister, who is responsible for unemployment opportunities, got away scot free while the government was scrambling to get the tories onto its side.
I can understand why the Conservatives want an adjournment at this time. The way it is going, they will not have a caucus in three weeks' time. In fact one of their members from Alberta, I believe the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone), said that all Conservative members from Alberta were offered some plums in the Liberal party. It is a sinister plan by the government to get rid of the official opposition. What Liberals cannot do in an election, they do after an election. They are trying to get them into the front benches. We have always said there was no difference between the two parties. Now it has been proven true.
April 6, 1977

Now dealing with the adjournment motion, we live in a society which talks about incentives. The economy must have incentives. What is the incentive for members of parliament to have a two-week break? What legislation has been tabled by the government? This break is a disincentive to do anything constructive about the problems facing the country. It has to be the height of cruelty.
Recently a report on youth and unemployment was put out by the Canadian Council on Social Development. It states that unemployment for youth is 14 per cent nationally and 16 per cent in the province of Quebec. That is an ominous percentage of young people unemployed in that province. What does the government bring forward? It brings forward a budget which states that the government cannot afford to solve unemployment in Canada. What a travesty on any responsible kind of government. It shows its members are bankrupt of any ideas. Then they come to the House and say we need a break. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) has his passage booked to the Bahamas. The hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campag-nola) has her passage booked to the Queen Charlotte Islands. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) is booked to look over his estates in Brazil. They are all set for the holidays.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wish to point out to the hon. member that the Queen Charlotte Islands is in my constituency. That is where this member of parliament will be over Easter. If the hon. member would hurry up his speech, we could get on with the business of serving the needs of the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that any Liberal would go back to his or her riding after that budget. 1 am surprised that they would have the gall to go back. I do not believe that many of them will go to their constituencies. They are all booked for the sunny south, the South Sea Islands.
Oh, oh!
The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has the floor for the purpose of making a speech. I suggest that he get on with it.
Hear, hear!

The government is asking us to consider an adjournment. Considering the extent to which some members of the government backbenches work, they do not deserve one day, let alone a ten day break. Very few of them attend committees and, when they do, they sit like bumps on logs. They do not speak in this House unless a motion of closure is introduced.
Let us look at what the government has produced since January 24 in terms of legislation. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) brought in a bill dealing with consumer credit. It was rather like an elephant. It was nine years in gestation, and then was a white elephant at that. It came before the House. There was no consultation on it. What we have is a white paper on consumer credit in the committee and it looks like it will be there for a while.
Easter Recess
What else did we get? We got an unemployment insurance bill. Far from doing anything constructive about unemployment it brought in a bill supposedly intended to tighten up the unemployment insurance program. What else have we got? We have the other part of the competition bill. That legislation, we are told, is taking a seldom used path; we are referring the subject matter to the committee, but not the bill.
To top it all, there was a budget which institutionalizes an unemployment rate resulting in one million being unemployed. Time was when we felt that an unemployment rate of 4 per cent was nearly disastrous for Canada. Eventually, though, we got to live with it; as a matter of fact we adjusted certain unemployment insurance payments to coincide with it. Now we have a sliding scale-a scale which is sliding ever upwards. There was a point at which we thought 6 per cent was disastrous. Now we are beginning to think of 6 per cent as an acceptable low level. The level is presently 8 per cent and it looks as though before the end of the year the Liberals will be prepared to regard 9 per cent unemployment as acceptable. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think a lot of them should be unemployed come the next election.
Hear, hear!

But what happens? They usually get appointed to boards or to commissions, or to the Senate. They do not run to be successful but to be defeated. There is more reward and more security in being defeated than in coming to the House and trying to do things here.
I see the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) giving me hand signals.
Explain!

I am going to get an explanation later. Unemployment is very cruel. The unfortunate thing is this: the government has created a psychology of dependency. It has said to the unemployed. "We shall provide you with adequate unemployment insurance payments or welfare payments or with some other form of income support, so it really doesn't matter what the unemployment rate is, we have cushioned the effect."
When a party like ours talks about a philosophy of full employment, believing that a man or a woman should work for what they are getting, people over on the other side say to us in very cynical tones. "Where is the money coming from?" That is always the question they ask. Really the question should be turned around. Where do they get the money at the present time to support the unemployed? What is it costing Canada to keep one million people on unemployment insurance, welfare, or some other form of support? I would put the figure at about $1 billion. What does it cost Canada in lost productivity? I would put that figure at about $7 billion. What does it cost Canada in lost taxes, taxes which would have been paid by all these people had they been employed? That figure alone would run into billions. The total amount of the loss is staggering.

April 6, 1977
Easter Recess
How then can we afford to give the corporate sector $1 billion in goodies with no assurance whatsoever that more employment will be created as a result?
The budget has created more loopholes than it has closed. At a time when the countries of the western world are moving to close loopholes in their tax systems this government is moving in the opposite direction by opening up loopholes for the corporate sector. No wonder the executive director of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce commented on the budget by saying, "We are smiling from ear to ear." Mr. Speaker, 1 went by the Rideau Club that night and I could hear singing coming from the club. I was walking home. They were all singing and drinking double scotches. I saw the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) there. He was there, and they were all singing "Happy days are here again."
Oh, oh!
We in this party have said time and time again that we are opposed to welfare handouts for the private sector. They have not shown they deserve it.
You don't know what you are talking about.
The hon. member, who comes from one of the Vancouver ridings, says I don't know what I am talking about.
Hear, hear!

I wasn't the one who appeared before a commission to present a brief on corporate concentration, and the commission said, "You don't know what you are talking about." If I present a brief to a commission, at least 1 read it. When the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) presents a brief to a commission he ought to know what it contains. When I present a brief, whether it is to the CRTC or to any other body, I at least participate in structuring it. When the hon. member presented one, one of the members of the commission said, "You ought to go and read your own brief." No wonder a member of the Conservative party can oil his way into the cabinet. Those are the parties of privilege.
Oh!

Anyway, Mr. Speaker, we do not wish to deny a vacation to the staff who keep this building going. After all, they got a big raise of 6 per cent. Some of them got a magnificent raise of 4 per cent! I would not want low paid members of parliament to keep these highly paid employees from having a break.
What about you?
The hon. member will please address the Chair.
Bearing in mind the need for those who work around the parliament buildings to have some sort of respite, I intend to conclude my remarks.
Hear, hear!

It is unfortunate that members on the government side will not be around their ridings to hear the complaints against the budget which was brought down a week ago. Suffice it to say that we in this party feel obliged to tell them, "You don't deserve a holiday at all!"
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) did not want to mislead the House regarding the Liberal members attending committee meetings and speaking on these committees. At present I am Deputy Chairman of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development; a member of the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry; a member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence-
And Jack Horner is in the cabinet!
I am also a member of the subcommittee of external affairs on international development-
Wonderful, wonderful!
Trudeau bypasses you and goes to Horner.
I am also a Canadian delegate to the Law of the Sea Conference.
Oh, oh!
You are also on the Standing Committee on the Restaurant of Parliament!

If the hon. member for Nickel Belt would check the reports of those standing committees he would find out that I, and many others on the Liberal side, spend a great deal of time questioning ministers and officials of the departments.
Is this a main speech?

I am sure the hon. member would not want to mislead the House regarding members on our side returning to our constituencies. I will be returning tomorrow to Comox-Alberni. It may interest the hon. member to know that in the next month I will be touring my riding with four cabinet ministers and spending approximately Five days during the Easter recess meeting with people.

You need their protection!
April 6, 1977
If the hon. member for Nickel Belt is going on holidays, let him say what he is doing; but let not that member impute motives to our side of the House, especially when those motives are incorrect.

Mr. Speaker, there is an important question being decided by this adjournment motion. While I am sympathetic to those members who have arranged many meetings in their ridings with cabinet ministers and others, there is an important matter to be settled. The matter involves the unemployment picture. There are a million people unemployed. If it were not for the decision of the official opposition, probably most members would be asked to stay here and discuss the problems affecting those who are unemployed and what we can do to put them back to work, whether it be through the budget or some other way.
We have an opportunity to tell the country that we are opposed to the callous treatment that a million Canadians are receiving, and that probably another 250,000 are going to receive when the schools empty this spring and they are unable to find work.
Easter Recess
an equal sum of money for those people who do not pay income tax and therefore are not getting any benefit and are unable to purchase goods and services. If they did that, it might do some good.
We have the opportunity of speaking and seeing that there is no Easter recess. That is a possibility. It is an exercise in which I have engaged previously. But because of the attitude of the official opposition, that would probably be self-defeating in that many of us would have to stay here with no hope of any accomplishment.
It is our intention to call a vote on the adjournment motion, and we will vote against it. If the official opposition wishes to vote for it and if the government members wish to vote for it, they will be saying they are not interested in staying in Ottawa to try to find some solution for those million to a million and a half who will be unemployed shortly.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.

My leader tells me that the figure is 400,000. Very few of them are going to find employment. It is a serious problem; it is a problem we feel the budget did not solve. The official opposition may have felt that the budget solved it, but they have agreed to support the budget that was presented.
There are several ways that we can make our point. As you know, a week or so ago we moved adjournment of the House. That was not the intention of the adjournment motion-

Well, my young friend may be a very competent lawyer in a school sense, but he has not been here very long.
